coverageDimensions: REGION: nothing enumerable. The page mentions Regions twice, but only to say the IAM Identity Center instance and the AWS managed application must be in a single Region and that support may vary by Region, then defers to other services' docs. No Region is named anywhere, so any per-Region figure attributed to this page is fabricated. SERVICE: partial and secondary only. The table's third column names 7 distinct values (IAM Identity Center, AWS Builder ID and IAM Identity Center, AWS Verified Access, Amazon Redshift, Amazon DataZone, NoSQL Workbench, AWS Transform), which resolve to 7 distinct services/identity sources if the compound cell is split. This is a per-scope qualifier, not a claim that these are all the services supported by IAM Identity Center, and the page makes no service-by-service coverage matrix. RESOURCE TYPE: nothing at all. No AWS resource types are named or enumerated on this page.

features.featureName: Access scopes supported by the IAM Identity Center OIDC service when registering a public client
features.reasoning: The scope string is the unit AWS enumerates and the unit a client actually requests, and 'accessScope' is the vocabulary name for exactly this list. It is catalogue-kind because the scope names are published by IAM Identity Center about itself, not drawn from a universe that exists without it. Rows do not collapse: all 12 scope strings are distinct, so expectedCount equals the row count and no distinctTargets field is needed.
features.scope: Second dimension present: the 'Services supported by' column, which names the service or identity source each scope applies to. Seven distinct cell values across the 12 rows: IAM Identity Center (1 row), AWS Builder ID and IAM Identity Center (6 rows), AWS Verified Access, Amazon Redshift, Amazon DataZone, NoSQL Workbench, AWS Transform (1 row each). A further qualifier appears in prose, not in the table: the whole table is scoped to registering a PUBLIC client, and the surrounding text notes these grant types work only with AWS services that support the capability and may not work in all Regions.
features.statuses: 12 supported, 0 not-supported, 0 partial; 12+0+0=12. The table is presence-only: every row is a scope AWS states the OIDC service supports for a public client. There is no status column, no Yes/No, no footnote marker and no exclusion note. Not-supported is entirely ABSENT on this axis, so no negative count may be derived. Read each row's presence as Supported; read nothing else as anything.

features.featureName: OAuth 2.0 grant flows supported for public clients
features.reasoning: The axis is the OAuth 2.0 grant flow, an IETF-standard universe that exists independently of IAM Identity Center, hence external. 'oauthGrantFlow' is a NEW axis name: nothing in the supplied vocabulary fits an OAuth grant-type enumeration, and forcing it into iamCapability or integrationType would misdescribe it. The unit of claim is one flow because AWS supports or does not support a flow as a whole.
features.scope: Two stated qualifiers: the flows are available only through AWS managed applications that support them, and the IAM Identity Center instance plus those applications must be deployed in a single AWS Region. The page also says these grant types work only with AWS services that support the capability and that support may vary by Region, then defers to each service's own documentation. So there is a per-service and per-Region scope acknowledged but NOT enumerated here.
features.statuses: 2 supported, 0 not-supported, 0 partial; 2+0+0=2. Two bullets under 'IAM Identity Center supports portions of the following OAuth 2.0 flows': Authorization Code Grant with PKCE (RFC 6749 / RFC 7636) and Device Authorization Grant (RFC 8628). Both are stated supported, with the hedge 'supports portions of', which a reader may treat as qualified support but which AWS does not break down per flow. Flows NOT listed (implicit grant, client credentials, resource owner password) are absent, never stated unsupported.
features.waived: Two grant flows is below the three-member floor for publishing an axis. The reading is right; the axis is too small for a denominator to mean anything.

pageTitle: Single sign-on access to SAML 2.0 and OAuth 2.0 applications
shouldNotExtract: The Topics list at the top (2 links) is navigation, not coverage. The two numbered step lists under 'Authorization Code Grant with PKCE' (4 steps) and 'Device Authorization Grant' (4 steps) are end-user walkthroughs; their nested bullets (2 and 3 items) describe what a consent screen displays and are not scopes or capabilities. 'Clients can specify a maximum of 25 scopes when requesting an access token' is a quota, not a count of supported scopes. The Description column of the table is prose, and the product names inside it (Kiro, Amazon CodeCatalyst) are not axis values. The note about clients using device.sso.{{region}}.amazonaws.com is migration advice. The RFC links, the console link and the OIDC API reference links are references. The whole 'See also' block about AI-coding-assistant skills and the agent-toolkit CLI command is boilerplate and states no coverage.
trap: The single most likely misparse: harvesting the 'Services supported by' column as the axis and reporting 12 services (or 7) as an IAM Identity Center service-coverage figure. It is a qualifier column on a scope table, one cell of which names two things at once ('AWS Builder ID and IAM Identity Center'), so both 12 and a naive distinct-string count of 7 misstate what the page claims. Runners-up: (1) reading '25 scopes' as the supported-scope count instead of the 12 table rows; (2) inventing a not-supported count for the scope table, which has no negative values at all; (3) treating the SAML sentence 'IAM Identity Center does not support validating signatures of incoming SAML authentication requests' as a row in some SAML feature matrix, when it is one isolated prose exclusion with no enumerated axis; (4) counting the 4+4 numbered consent steps or their nested bullets as capabilities; (5) pulling product names out of the Description column (Kiro, CodeCatalyst) as axis values; (6) reading 'supports portions of the following OAuth 2.0 flows' as Partial status per flow when AWS gives no per-flow breakdown.
whatThePageStates: This is mostly a concept page. It explains that IAM Identity Center gives users single sign-on access to SAML 2.0 or OAuth 2.0 applications, then describes SAML 2.0 in prose and OAuth 2.0 in more detail. Two enumerations carry a real coverage claim: a two-bullet list of the OAuth 2.0 grant flows IAM Identity Center supports (Authorization Code Grant with PKCE, Device Authorization Grant), and a 12-row table titled 'Access scopes supported by the IAM Identity Center OIDC service when registering a public client' that names each scope, its description, and the service or identity source it is supported by. The rest is walkthrough material: two numbered step lists describing the end-user consent experience for each grant flow. The page also carries one stated exclusion in prose ('IAM Identity Center does not support validating signatures of incoming SAML authentication requests from SAML applications'), but that is a single sentence, not an enumerated axis, so it is not counted as a feature.
